metadata.title: One bacterium, forty-four hours
metadata.author: PALS's Notes
metadata.description: A thought experiment: one E. coli cell doubling every 20 minutes with nothing to stop it would outweigh the Earth in about 44 hours. It never happens: the food runs out. Drawn cell, computed masses, schematic growth curve.

meta.name: source
meta.value: Sezonov, Joseleau-Petit and D'Ari 2007 (20 minutes in rich broth at 37 C; growth stops for lack of a carbon source); Earth's mass 5.972e24 kg; arithmetic in tools/calc.py

text.text: Here is why it never does.
DRAWN · NOT TO SCALE · WARM, WELL FED
CDC / E. SOWERS, J. HANEY CARR

cue.text: Food going off? Do the sums.
One bacterium, dividing every twenty minutes,
would outweigh the Earth in under two days.
Here is why it never does.
Given everything it needs, it can split
in two in as little as twenty minutes.
Twenty minutes later, four.
An hour in: eight.
Now a thought experiment.
Suppose nothing ever stopped it:
food without end, room without end.
After ten hours, all of them together
weigh about a milligram.
After twenty hours: roughly a tonne.
And in about forty-four hours,
they would outweigh the Earth.
It never happens.
Long before that, the food runs out,
and the doubling slows and stops.
That is why no population can keep doubling:
every doubling needs something to eat.
